nameStory: White beggarticks gets its name from its sneaky seeds that literally beg to come along for the ride! The seeds have two sharp, barbed projections (called awns) that grab onto clothing, fur, and anything else that brushes by, earning them the nickname 'shepherd's needles' and 'Spanish needles.' The 'white' part refers to the bright white petals that surround the yellow center, distinguishing it from its many relatives.
description: White beggarticks is a weedy wildflower that looks like a small, scrappy daisy with bright white petals surrounding a golden-yellow center. This annual or short-lived perennial plant typically grows 1-3 feet tall with branching stems and opposite leaves. It's part of the huge sunflower family and loves disturbed areas where it can quickly establish itself. Despite being considered a weed, it produces cheerful white flowers that butterflies and other pollinators enjoy visiting.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: The real giveaway - flat, dark brown seeds with two sharp, barbed projections that stick aggressively to clothing and feel scratchy when you try to remove them

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Classic daisy-like blooms about 1 inch across with 5-8 pure white petals (ray flowers) surrounding a bright yellow center that feels slightly fuzzy to touch

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite leaves that are deeply divided into 3-5 narrow segments, giving them a feathery appearance and feeling somewhat rough when rubbed

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Upright, much-branched plant that forms bushy clumps and can quickly take over disturbed ground with its spreading growth pattern

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Square-ish green stems that feel firm and slightly ridged when rolled between your fingers, often with a reddish tinge at the joints

habitat: White beggarticks thrives in disturbed soils like roadsides, abandoned lots, field edges, and garden borders throughout New England. It particularly loves areas with rich, moist soil that gets plenty of sun, though it can tolerate some shade. You'll often find it mixed with other weedy species in areas that have been recently disturbed by human activity.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge as small rosettes with their characteristic divided leaves becoming visible in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with bright white daisy-like flowers appearing continuously from mid-summer onward, attracting various pollinators.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and become the plant's most noticeable feature, readily sticking to anything that passes by. Plants may continue blooming until first frost.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, but their persistent seeds remain scattered on the ground and stuck to nearby vegetation.

funFact: The young leaves are actually edible and taste similar to spinach when cooked - many tropical cultures use them as a nutritious leafy vegetable, and they're packed with vitamins A and C!
confusionNotes: White beggarticks can be confused with other white-flowered daisies, but those telltale barbed seeds are unmistakable - if it grabs your socks and won't let go, you've found beggarticks! Remember: 'Barbed beggarticks stick and pick.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite its reputation as a troublesome weed in North America, white beggarticks is valued in many parts of the world as both food and medicine. The name 'Spanish needles' can be confusing since it's not from Spain and isn't related to actual needles - it just refers to the sharp, needle-like seed projections.
compareHints: White beggarticks stands out from its many beggarticks relatives because of its prominent white petals - most other species in the genus have small, inconspicuous flowers or yellow petals. While devil's beggarticks and nodding beggarticks have similar barbed seeds, they lack the showy white ray flowers that make this species look like a proper daisy.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many beggarticks species, Devil's Beggarticks is distinguished by its three-part leaves (versus simple leaves in Nodding Beggarticks) and its lack of showy petals (unlike the bright yellow rays of Tickseed Sunflower).

Among New England's many beggarticks species, Nodding Beggarticks is the easiest to identify because of its drooping flowers - Devil's Beggarticks has upward-facing flowers and deeply divided leaves, while Smooth Beggarticks has much larger, showier flowers that face outward.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Purplestem stands out for its smooth stems with purple coloring and relatively few flower heads per plant.
Unlike its weedy beggarticks relatives that grow in damp soil and are known for their sticky seeds, Water Marigold is the aquatic specialist of the family.
Among New England's beggarticks, Tall Beggarticks stands out for its height and hairy stems.

Unlike its freshwater cousins like Devil's Beggarticks or Nodding Beggarticks, Estuary Beggarticks has evolved to handle salt stress, giving it thicker, more succulent leaves and limiting it to coastal habitats.

Among its many Bidens relatives in New England, Smooth Beggarticks stands out for its simple, undivided leaves (unlike Three-parted Beggarticks) and its prominent yellow ray petals (unlike Devil's Beggarticks which often lacks showy petals entirely).

Among its many beggarticks relatives, swamp beggarticks stands out for its complete lack of ray petals (the showy outer petals), unlike nodding beggarticks or smooth beggarticks which have yellow rays.

Among New England beggarticks, Three-parted is unique for its deeply three-divided leaves - Devil's Beggarticks has simple oval leaves, while Spanish Needles has finely divided, almost fern-like foliage.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Tickseed Sunflower stands out for having showy yellow petals - many of its relatives like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.

Among its beggarticks relatives, Spanish needles stands out with its finely divided, feathery leaves - most other Bidens species have simple oval leaves or leaves divided into just 3-5 broad segments.
Among New England's beggarticks, Bearded Beggarticks stands out for its large, showy yellow petals - most other species like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.

Marsh Tickseed stands out from its beggarticks relatives by being strictly a wetland specialist - while cousins like Devil's Beggarticks grow in disturbed soils and gardens, Marsh Tickseed demands consistently soggy conditions.
Among its many beggarticks relatives, Eaton's is unique for its salt marsh habitat - most others prefer freshwater wetlands or disturbed soils.
